sweep_summary: Portuguese (port1283) is in the catalog as weight-hedged on Wetzels 2007. Nothing contradicts the classification. Confirming/refining first-hand statements read: Garcia 2017 Phonology (postprint; weight rule + Houaiss counts; best new statement), Carvalho 1989 (moraic restatement; final /-s/ not heavy), Cantoni 2013 thesis and Cantoni 2008 (three-syllable window, penult default, ASPA type frequencies 67/18/15), Bisol 1994 and Lee 1994 (Letras de Hoje scans, scanned: the original weight rule and the morphological weight-insensitive alternative), Lu et al. 2018 and Frota et al. 2020 (EP: 74% penult / 23% final / 3% antepenult types; window), Guzzo 2018, Guzzo & Garcia 2021, Butler & Frota 2018 (window / penult-most-frequent only); Wetzels 2007 re-downloaded and the catalog quote verified verbatim (p. 32). Secondary-stress papers (Moraes 2003, Arantes & Barbosa 2006, Fernandes-Svartman 2012, Lee 2002, Collischonn 1994) and Santos 2003 / Moraes 2008 are silent on primary placement. Not obtainable: Veiga et al. 2013 (Springer JS challenge; abstract only), Castelo 2005 and Correia 2009 (ULisboa repository timed out), Roca 1999, Vigário 2003, Sandalo 2006, Frota & Vigário 2001 etc. (de Gruyter/Benjamins/JSTOR/SAGE paywalls), Schwindt 2001 and Abaurre & Galves 1998 (SciELO 403), print-only Pereira 1999 (highest acquisition priority: EP book-length metrical analysis), Pereira & Araujo 2007, Walters 1994, Delgado Martins 1982. all discovery went through Semantic Scholar/Crossref APIs, journal archives and repository endpoints. sources.quote: Portuguese word stress is quantity sensitive: final heavy syllables are stressed in the unmarked case, and prefinal heavy syllables can never be skipped by the stress rule. Secondary stress is not sensitive to syllable weight, is assigned from right to left, and is lexically irrelevant. In Hayes' model, primary stress would very probably be described as non-iterative, right to left footing. The relevant foot is the moraic trochee. [...] Antepenultimate stress is exceptional, even in words which end in a sequence of two open syllables. Therefore, a lexical diacritic is used to mark the final syllable in a word like abobora as extrametrical. Equally, the exceptionality of prefinal stress in words which end in a heavy syllable is accounted for by a diacritic which marks the final mora as extrametrical.

Data from the FrePOP database (Frota et al. 2010), containing 1,486,092 prosodic words from spoken and written language, shows that 74% of words with two syllables or more are stressed on the penultimate syllable, 23% of words are stressed on the final syllable, and 2% of words have stress on the antepenultimate syllable. [...] Nonetheless, duration is found to be the most robust correlate of stress among the five cues examined in this study. However, the effect of duration is found to be limited to certain vowels and speakers (i.e. Group 1, Group 2, and Group 3), and sometimes obscured by intonation contours (i.e. Group 4). F0, F1, F2, and intensity, for almost all the cases, do not signal stress.

sources.citation: Frota, Sónia, Joseph Butler, Ertugrul Uysal, Cátia Severino & Marina Vigário (2020). European Portuguese-learning infants look longer at iambic stress: New data on language specificity in early stress perception. Frontiers in Psychology 11: 1890.
sources.quote: EP has variable stress, similarly to English, Spanish, Catalan, and Hebrew (but unlike French or Finnish). Stress may fall within the last three syllables of the prosodic word and it can distinguish between lexical items (e.g., bambo [ˈbɐ̃bu] / bambu [bɐ̃ˈbu], 'lax' / 'bamboo'; explícito / explicito 'explicit' / 'I make explicit'). ... The frequency of trochaic disyllabic words in EP varies between 66 and 74% in adult speech and 63 and 70% in child-directed speech ... the traditional dominant view in the literature on EP assumes that penultimate stress is the common stress pattern (Viana et al., 1996).
sources.note: Infant perception study; describes EP stress as variable, contrastive, within a three-syllable right-edge window, penultimate most common; no weight rule.

sources.quote: In BP, primary stress is assigned to the ultimate, penultimate, or antepenultimate syllables (Mattoso-Camara Jr., 1953; Bisol, 1992). Among the stress patterns for BP words, penultimate stress is predominant: For 2-4 syllable words, it occurs in more than 70% of all stress positions (Cantoni, 2008; Frota, Vigario, & Martins, 2010). In contrast, the frequencies of ultimate and penultimate stress are about 20% and 5%.
